Text: Life is like a TV series that keeps getting renewed for a new season [SEP] I'm 33 years old. I remember so many different ages of my life. 13, 18, 22, 27...I remember thinking that I was so old at these times and that whatever I was going through at the time was so monumentally important. But life just...persists. It keeps going on and on, long after you expect it to stop. Most people agree that The Simpsons was best in seasons 3-9ish, but yet it kept getting renewed and there's new stories every season. Life is kind of like that, yet you don't have a choice but to keep watching. You can't turn it off, long after the writing becomes derivative and boring. You are forced to keep your eyes glued to the screen for season 28, season 39, season 47... I mean, like Camus talks about, the meaning of life is what stops a person from ending it. You could willingly forgo the whole process and end it if you wanted. Frankly, I'm not going to do that. I'm going to keep persisting on through the years. I just find it odd how important everything seems, and then everyone just moves on. Fashion, music, movies, TV, memes, etc. everything seems so important, and then 5 years later it's in the dustbin of history. It makes you start to become sort of numb to all of these changes, because you know that it's all temporary and there's always going to be a new season next year.

Now, I understand fully that nothing can be proven...but I am quite interested in the issue of determinism and derive pleasure from arguing about its logic. While the belief in free will, just as that of religion, makes people happy in a depressing universe (not intrinsically so, but because of human biology), I can take no solace in a fact because I rightly know that both religion and free will were made up by humans, to explain existence and to cope with existential questioning. When you die your life starts over again from the beginning [SEP] Time has essentially been proven to be non-liner. We live in a deterministic block universe. The only differences between past, present, and future are within the constructs of your mind. There is no such thing as _x001C_now_x001D_ as every point in time is equally real. As such, you_x0019_re simply a time-slice which exists eternally and is experiencing a subjective flow of time. Once your conscious is terminated your perception of reality starts from the beginning. The same life you_x0018_ve already lived plays out again. There was never a time when you didn_x0019_t exist and they_x0019_ll never be a time when you cease to exist, you_x0019_re just exist eternally trapped within your own slice of space-time. I believe this is the only fully coherent view on the nature of existence. The idea that you didn_x0019_t exist before you were born and will cease to exist doesn_x0019_t make sense. If you only exist for finite amount of time and don_x0019_t exist for an infinite amount of time the odds of you existing right now are zero. This model of existence also solves the hard problem of consciousness as it makes conscious experience inherent to the universe in a way that simply slides in with the rest of what we know about space-time without coming up with stuff like _x001D_that chair over there has a certain level of consciousness_x001C_. If there are any good counter agreements to this claim I_x0019_d love to here them, but I think this is the strongest model on the nature of existence and I_x0019_ve yet to hear anything else more sensible.

How I got out of my existential crisis a year ago. [SEP] I was talking to a friend today about the existential crisis that I had last year. It was one of the most, of the the most challenging experience that I have ever faced. There was, however, a very, very happy ending. I figured it would give some hope to the people here. Three years ago, after many many things going wrong in my life, internally and externally, I was having insane levels of stress. After months of that, I started experiencing derealization. For you guys that are not aware, derealization is a defense mechanism that our mind uses when we are passing through a lot of negative emotion. It turns off the prt of the brain that makes you accept life as how it is and be "inserte" in it,making you realize how absurd reality is. Since I was in a very, very introspective and desperate state, this realization did not help me. I began by questioning who, or, in that case what I was. Was I anything? Who am I to determine if I am anything at all? Does anything exist? As most of you guys know, it becomes almost impossible to live when you "know" that life is a fraud. I started missing being worried about "planet earth" things. Thankfully, my therapist was a anthropologist with a big philosophy background. He didn't want me to read philosophy or take me out of the crisis, instead, he said what I was going through, although painful, was something great that most people run from. He guided me through the whole questioning, making me find the cues myself. It was a great experience, I had the task to philosophize and come up with the answers that humans came up with thousands of years ago. Which "thought" got me out? I drew in my head two realities: the "real reality", which would be the truth: things have no meaning or quality. And the "human reality", which would be our body creating a lens that distorts the world and creates quality. This difference in "size"(the nothingness is a lot bigger than our life) bothered me. I, however, realized that difference was insignificant since it is our human minds that create this comparison. In the universe, nothing matters. I, after suffering a shit ton for months, had to kneel down to how things are and accept that life is just an experience. This acceptance triggered my recovery and turned me into a very, very optimistic person. I accepted my insignificance in an already insignificant world.

Compatibilist desert: a modest claim that misses the point [SEP] The free will debate isn_x0019_t primarily a metaphysical curiosity about what kinds of causation are possible in the universe, even though this curiosity may be satisfied by the core of the debate: **whether and when we can hold people responsible** for praise or blame. We commonly use the term "*morally* responsible", but this can be misguiding, because it may seem that we depend on moral realism being true, but we **do not**. That is, actions need not be "right" or "wrong" in an objective, independent sense, they only need to be "right" or "wrong" in relation to a goal that may go against our interests or likings. For example, we can imagine a society that has declared a certain word forbidden. There is nothing *inherently wrong* about saying it, they have just decided that it is wrong. Yet when one utters the word in such society, the question *at the heart of the free will debate* is whether we can hold that person responsible. Responsible in what way? There is a crucial distinction between affirming the person is to blame *simply in virtue of having performed an action* (basic-desert responsibility) and affirming they are to blame because *it will have positive effects* such as deterrence or rehabilitation (forward-looking or consequentialist responsibility). Assuming for the moment that the free will debate is about basic-desert, the argument is surprisingly simple (for our purposes, *agent* is a metaphysically neutral term: a being capable of acting intentionally, i.e., performing actions for reasons, in light of beliefs and desires): *1.* An agent deserves blame simply for performing an action if and only if the ultimate causal source of that action lies within them. In other words, their will must be free from factors beyond their control, such as the remote past, the laws of nature (deterministic *or* indeterministic), or their chemical makeup at the moment of choice, itself shaped by genetic, environmental, and stochastic factors. *2.* The causal source of an agent's actions does not lie wholly within them; their will is not free from factors beyond their control. *3.* Therefore, an agent does not deserve blame simply for performing any action. This is a simple *modus tollens* and logically valid. The **source incompatibilist** conclusion follows from its premises, so any quarrel with the argument concerns the truth of these, and we can sidestep the usual confusion about determinism_x0019_s supposed consequences. I'm happy to concede that there is true contingency in the world and that any choice is not inevitable in principle. However, once it occurs, it is produced by specific causal factors (our desire, our memories, brain states, etc., **or even the libertarian agent-cause**). This said, I suppose that premise *1* will be quite uncontroversial for **libertarians**, who will surely deny premise *2*. A denial that usually is at the centre of the free will debate and should revolve around defending the freedom of the will from the relevant factors and not solely around the tedious debate about determinism. Sure, determinism being false is a necessary condition to deny premise *2*, *but not sufficient*. Neither is our awareness about choosing, or the fact that we can imagine choosing something else, although this makes the libertarian position comprehensible: we choose to lift our left hand and then can easily imagine choosing the right one instead. Premise *1* is left for **strong compatibilists** to tackle, and just to be clear, in denying premise *1*, one is asserting that we deserve blame simply in virtue of performing any action, although our will is not free from factors beyond our control. It_x0019_s a tough position. Even if our action issues from our own reasons-responsive mechanism, my stance is that *we still cannot be morally responsible in the basic-desert sense if the mechanism_x0019_s existence and operation are ultimately due to factors beyond our control. So ownership or identification doesn_x0019_t solve the problem, it just pushes the lack of control one level deeper*. Faced with this problem, some adopt a **moderate compatibilism** and ignore the argument altogether, shifting the debate to focus on forward-looking responsibility, because in that way premise *1* is easily denied; for this kind of responsibility the will doesn't need to be free from factors beyond the agent's control, it merely has to be free from certain factors in certain moments. Free will is now circumstantial. The argument is now: *1.* An agent deserves blame in a way that brings about a positive outcome (such as deterrence or rehabilitation) if and only if their will is free from coercion or manipulation by other agents, and from undue influences such as mental disorders. *2.* There are cases in which an agent's will is free from such factors, and cases in which it is not. *3.* Therefore, in some cases an agent deserves blame of this kind, and in others they do not. This is a simple *modus ponens* and logically valid. The conclusion follows from its premises so, once more, any quarrel with the argument concerns truth of these. But the argument is now toothless. This is the cost of shifting to forward-looking responsibility. Who would have any problem with this argument? Premise *2* is obviously true, and *even libertarians* can accept premise *1*, because it_x0019_s merely instrumental. A libertarian believes the agent deserves blame simply in virtue of performing the action, and yet can agree that, even if they didn't deserve it, the agent must be blamed in a forward-looking way to prevent future harm if his will is free from coercion from other agents. In summary, the free will debate is about elucidating whether and when we can hold people responsible for praise or blame *just because of what we_x0019_ve done*, which reflects a metaphysical fact about us and our freedom. It is not about blaming because doing so will have good effects. This sidesteps the real issue. It hijacks the free will debate entirely. If that is what interests you, you are barking up the wrong tree.

A deterministic system does not need to be perfectly or even remotely predictable by humans [SEP] Disclaimer: This is all AI generated, soo no need to take it seriously(I guess, idk) Reasons deterministic systems can be unpredictable * **Chaotic systems:** A chaotic system is a deterministic system with an extreme sensitivity to its initial conditions. Known as the "butterfly effect," a tiny, unmeasurable difference in the initial state can lead to wildly divergent and unpredictable outcomes over time. For instance, despite being governed by deterministic physics, it is impossible for humans to accurately predict the weather long-term. * **Incomplete information:** A human trying to predict a system will always have incomplete or imprecise knowledge of its initial state. The more variables and complexity a system has, the more impossible it becomes to measure all of them with perfect accuracy. This finite precision, when applied to a chaotic system, ensures that long-term predictions will become worthless. * **Computational limits:** A system's future might be determined, but calculating it can be computationally impossible. For example, the three-body problem_x0014_describing the movement of three gravitational bodies_x0014_has no general closed-form solution, making long-term prediction impossible even though the system is deterministic. * **Recursive prediction:** In some cases, the very act of making a prediction influences the outcome, making it impossible to predict accurately. A person or system that is part of a larger deterministic system cannot predict its own future from within because the prediction itself is a new physical event in the causal chain. * **The Halting Problem:** In computer science, a deterministic program's future state is determined by its code. However, the Halting Problem proves there is no universal algorithm that can determine whether every possible program will finish running or get stuck in an infinite loop. This demonstrates that even a simple deterministic system can contain an uncomputable or unpredictable element.

I have remained silent throughout the entire thing. Any time someone brings her up, or asks what happened, I only reply with I wish her the best and have nothing negative to say about her, or say nothing at all. It_x0019_s amazing how much happier and at peace I feel lately to mind my own business and not get involved in any drama. A few years ago, before being introduced to stoic philosophy, this would have gone much uglier. I have quickly learned how much power is in utter silence. Edit to add: I don_x0019_t necessarily view this as revenge. I don_x0019_t want to get revenge, because I genuinely care about her as a person and want the best for her; despite how immensely disappointed I was. I am more or less proud of how far I_x0019_ve come in this stoic journey of mine- since 2 years ago I know I absolutely would have sought revenge on her in an ugly manner for doing this. Free will lacks any explanatory power that isn't explained more simply by the lack thereof. [SEP] The explanation for human behavior with the fewest moving parts is hard determinism or the lack of free will. Everything can be explained easily by our past experiences. There's no reason to further complicate things with half-cocked ideas about agents causing things when everything is easily explained by the past. Therefore according to occam's razor it is the most likely explanation. Free will involves adding an interstitial agent to the stream of causation. The problem is, this agent's actions must be determined by either the agent's past or something inherent to the agent that was given to it by it's creator. There are no other data streams for this agent to base its choices off of. Basic desert moral responsibility is thus impossible to establish. Free will is not necessary to understand a person's actions and may actually make them make less sense.

Free Will is for the bird brained [SEP] Free Will is for the Birds: How Crows, Parrots, and Bowerbirds Are Rebuilding Our Understanding of Choice We tend to think of free will_x0014_the ability to make a conscious choice between options_x0014_as the pinnacle of human exceptionalism. We weigh pros and cons, deliberate on the future, and then (maybe) act. But what if that very ability, the one we hold so dear, is actually a fairly common piece of cognitive technology? What if, to find its roots, we just need to look up at the trees? The more we study our feathered friends, the more the evidence points in one direction: free will isn't a gift given only to humans. It's a survival strategy that evolved first in the birds. **The Crows: The Meta-Learning Masterminds** If you want to see raw, analytical decision-making in action, look no further than the corvid family. Crows don't just react to the world; they think about it. Take the famous Aesop's fable experiments. When presented with a tube of water partially filled with a floating worm just out of reach, a crow doesn't just peck at the glass futilely. It pauses. It assesses. It then drops stones into the tube to raise the water level. This isn't just tool use; it's causal reasoning. The crow is visualizing the future outcome of an action it hasn't taken yet. Even more compelling is the work done by neurobiologist Andreas Nieder, which showed that crows possess "primary consciousness." When a crow makes a choice in a task, its brain activity isn't just a mechanical response to a stimulus. The neurons fire in a way that suggests subjective experience_x0014_they are aware of what they are deciding. That moment of hesitation before a crow solves a puzzle? That's the ghost in the machine, pulling the lever. But crows aren't just forward thinkers. They're also historians. Crows remember faces. Not "humans generally." Your face. Specifically. Among thousands. Retained for years. When wronged, they don't just avoid you. They organize. They tell the murder. (Yes, a group of crows is called a murder. The etymology is doing work here.) The murder reaches a verdict. They teach their children. Children who have never met you. Already know you're the problem. This is not instinct. Instinct doesn't require: - Individual recognition - Social transmission of specific grievance - Generational continuation of targeted response This is a fatwa. Issued by birds. Executed across generations. Against one specific human. Who probably just touched a nest once. **The Bowerbirds: The Aesthetic Architects** If crows represent the "will" part of free will, bowerbirds represent the "free" part. Specifically, they demonstrate freedom of expression. Male bowerbirds build elaborate structures_x0014_not nests, but art installations_x0014_to attract a mate. They aren't just following a genetic blueprint. If they were, all bowers of a given species would look identical. Instead, they are interior decorators with attitude. They carefully choose objects based on color, arranging them in specific patterns to create forced perspective illusions that make them look bigger and more appealing to females. But the real magic is in the theft. When a bowerbird sees his neighbor has a cooler, brighter blue object than he does, he doesn't just get jealous. He formulates a plan. He waits until the neighbor is gone, sneaks over, and steals it. This requires a complex understanding of "theory of mind"_x0014_the ability to recognize that another bird has something you want, and that their absence is your opportunity. That's not instinct; that's a calculated, individual choice driven by personal desire. **The Grey Parrots: The Logic of Language** Finally, we have the African Grey Parrots, immortalized by Dr. Irene Pepperberg's work with Alex. Alex didn't just mimic human speech; he used it to make requests and, crucially, to refuse. Alex could identify objects, colors, and materials. But more importantly, he understood the concept of "same" and "different"_x0014_abstract categories that require higher-order thinking. When presented with a tray of objects and asked "What's the same?," he had to scan, analyze, and choose a category to report. When shown an apple for the first time_x0014_no trained word available_x0014_Alex didn't stay silent. He combined what he knew. He called it a "banerry." Banana. Cherry. Closest available concepts. Novel word. Novel object. Problem solved. That's not mimicry. That's combinatorial creativity. That's language doing what language actually does: generating new meaning from existing parts. **The Last Thing Alex Said** The night before he died unexpectedly, Irene Pepperberg put him in his cage as usual. Alex said: *"You be good. I love you. You'll be here tomorrow?"* His standard goodbye. She said yes. He wasn't there tomorrow. Determinists, please explain: *"You be good."* That's a moral instruction. From a bird. To a human. Which prior physical cause determined: - That "good" is a relevant category - That Irene specifically needed reminding - That this moment warranted saying it - The love **Conclusion** So, what do crows, bowerbirds, and parrots tell us? They tell us that free will isn't a metaphysical ghost in a biological machine. It's a practical tool. It's the ability to run a simulation of the future (crows), to execute a generational fatwa against a specific human (also crows), to express individual aesthetic preference (bowerbirds), and to use symbolic communication_x0014_including invented words_x0014_to alter your reality (parrots). If you want to see what free will actually looks like, stop looking at philosophy books and start looking at bird feeders. Free will is for the birds. *"You be good."* *Alex knew.* =& _x001B_>=& _x001B_

It's nonsensical **OUGHT:** Okay, free will doesn't exist, what ought we do about it? And here we get a whole host of arguments about how bad or dangerous it is to not believe in free will, morality, our purpose, etc. All very concerning and interesting questions, but has NO BEARING on the true/false factor of the IS question. So DON'T conflate the two! You can't use arguments from the OUGHT section to then say therefore the IS question must be true. This is just straight up irrational argument. If I was dictator of this sub I'd be mandating every discussion clarifying which section they're in in order to keep argumentation clear on this topic!

My list of rules for a stoic life. [SEP] A few years ago I wrote down two handfuls of guiding principles or rules that would give me some kind of safety rails for life, something I could turn to when I was facing the frequent uncertainty of how to act in difficult situations but also in day to day existence. Most of what I wrote down were lessons I learned from reading Marcus and Seneca but there was also inspiration from Miyamoto Musashi's [DokkMdM]( (where I got the idea to make a list) and principles of Zen Buddhism that got thrown in there. I don_x0019_t claim to have any profound answers or that these rules are even close to the most important one should adhere to, but they have helped me tremendously and on the chance that someone else might also find value in them I thought I_x0019_d share them. So without further ado, here's the list: &#x200B; 1. **To dedicate your life to something, even if it lacks meaning to others.** 2. **The process is the goal, every action, however seemingly meaningless should be performed with great care. You are building your own temple, chop wood, carry water.** 3. **Nature has given you emotions so that they can be of use to you, so observe them and let only those come to the surface that are of service to you.** 4. **Take care of your body and your mind, for the body is your vessel and your mind it_x0019_s operator.** 5. **To not be roused by distressing events or by other peoples actions and treatment of you for you cannot change them. But to care deeply about how you respond and how you treat them.** 6. **To not attach yourself to material possessions and simple pleasures and to not mourn the loss of them. To be as fulfilled living in a hut as in a palace. But to also recognize that abolishing material pleasures completely is not desirable, and to enjoy them in disciplined moderation.** 7. **To be complete in yourself. To not depend on anyone for happiness or completion.** 8. **To accept and understand but not to succumb to your preconceived notions.** 9. **To recognize the potential for goodness and evil in everyone as in yourself.** 10. **If one has to think of the past or the future it should be a deliberate practice, otherwise one should not dwell on what will be or what has been and be present.**

Linguistic issues with free will [SEP] My 3 year old says she is not free when I am physically restraining her, and that she is free when I let go. Freedom here is not in any way theoretical. There is no reason to believe my 3 year old is wrong, or that she has secret theories about the nature of causality. The meaning of free in this common usage is in how it_x0019_s used, not in theory. It_x0019_s not theoretical because we can point to it. _x001C_This is free, this is not._x001D_ Whether any kind of freedom is contra-causal is an entirely different theoretical matter. If a skeptic wants to come in and explain how *actually that_x0019_s not freedom*, you_x0019_d also have to agree that there_x0019_s no difference between being a slave and being a slaver. You_x0019_d be losing an argument with a 3 year old as she screams over and over what she means by _x001C_free_x001D_. It_x0019_s quite absurd to reject this common meaning of the word. In fact, if you did this, and argued that *no possible distinction can be made between what we call free and not free,* that it would arguably undermine your ability to make any distinctions, and force yourself into performative contradiction. Or you would have to claim that _x001C_free_x001D_ is so tainted by contra-causality that we shouldn_x0019_t use it. But you_x0019_d still have to differentiate between one who is physically in chains and one who is able to act as they will, and you would have to come up with new terminology that would mean exactly what my 3 year old already meant by _x001C_free_x001D_. If we accept the obvious, that _x001C_free_x001D_ is something intelligible that we can point to, understand, and define, then without question, the will can be free in the same way anything can. Again, if you deny this, you would have to say the same of being in chains or not. One would be constrained to be a slaver just as much as one is constrained to be a slave. As soon as we differentiate between these two, we can do the same with the will. It seems then like the only ground free will skeptics have to stand on is to reject _x001C_Free Will_x001D_ as a term that has too much baggage in its connection to contra-causality. But this is really a linguistic problem. We can have _x001C_free will_x001D_ even if we don_x0019_t have _x001C_Free Will_x001D_. This puts us in a linguistic predicament where we may want to be able to talk about the will and the ways in which it is and can be _x001C_free_x001D_ but, I don_x0019_t want to be confused for contra-causal _x001C_Free Will._x001D_ So to those who say compatibilism is just redefining _x001C_Free Will_x001D_, I would say no, Libertarian Free Will redefined _x001C_free_x001D_ in conjunction with _x001C_will_x001D_ into a theoretical philosophical term. Compatibilism reclaims it and restores it to its common meaning: yes, _x001C_free_x001D_ is an adjective that can be applied to _x001C_will_x001D_. It_x0019_s actually not a deep, theoretical matter. And on top of that, free will skeptics are actually the ones using theoretical redefinitions of common language. _x001C_Choice_x001D_ and _x001C_control_x001D_ are obviously possible as they are commonly used. It_x0019_s only by redefining them into philosophical theories that you perform the linguistic illusion that allows you to say _x001C_you don_x0019_t choose_x001D_ or _x001C_you don_x0019_t have control._x001D_ This is clearly false if we_x0019_re talking about how the words are commonly used.

Beyond the Determinism vs. Indeterminism False Dichotomy: A Case for Semi-Determinism and free will [SEP] In most discussions of free will, we are forced into two rigid corners: 1. **Determinism:** The universe is a clock. Every choice is "destined" and agents have no freedom to do otherwise. 2. **Indeterminism:** The universe is a dice roll. Cause and effect don't exist, so choices aren't meaningful because they have no reliable bearing on outcomes. As these ideas are usually presented, neither allows for true free will. I believe this is a **false dichotomy**. It ignores a fundamental reality: **stochasticity (randomness) and structure are not mutually exclusive.** # The Middle Ground: Semi-Determinism I propose a model called **Semi-determinism**. In this view, stochasticity is a fundamental property of the universe, but it is strictly **constrained and biased** by physical laws (thermodynamics, electromagnetism, and physical structure). * **Biased Stochasticity:** Particles don_x0019_t just behave randomly; they operate within a set of possible states biased by the laws of the universe. For example, particles are more likely to move toward thermodynamic equilibrium than away from it. * **The Appearance of Determinism:** Macro-level events appear deterministic because of the **Law of Large Numbers**. When trillions of probabilistic micro-events are averaged together, they create highly predictable behaviors_x0014_like how we can predict a half-life without knowing when a single atom will decay. * **Structural Effects:** How these events combine changes the outcome. **Aggregation** (like particles forming a solid) narrows the range of possibilities toward stability, while **chaining events** (like a decision-tree) can widen them. # Life as a "Bias-Engine" We see this most clearly in biology. Life requires a balance of stability (preserving successful traits) and exploration (trying new things). In my research, I look at how organisms use physical structures to actively **bias the probability distributions** of future events. A clear example is cellular reproduction: some regions of the chromosome are structured to reduce errors (preserving critical genes) while others allow for more variation. # A Path to Free Will and Consciousness Semi-determinism offers the two things necessary for agency that the old models lack: * **Freedom:** Multiple futures are physically possible because the underlying substrate is not fixed. * **Continuity:** The outcome isn't a random "coin flip." The **agent** acts as the structure that biases these probabilities in real-time to influence the outcome. I_x0019_ve written a full paper detailing this "Semi-deterministic" model, looking at how agents function as a "Silent Auction" of competing influences to navigate a world that is neither a clock nor a chaos. The 3 Stoic Disciplines [SEP] Ive noticed many of the posts here have become people seeking advice or talking about their personal experiences wherein they apply Stoicism. However I see very few posts regarding the original logical dialectic, references to Stoic texts, etc. I seek to give people tangible and practical ways in which they can apply stoicism to their lives, and Ill do so here by explaining the three disciplines. Epictetus described a threefold division between *lived* stoic practice. 1. The Discipline of Desire, which has to do with acceptance of our fate 2. The Discipline of Action, which has to do with philanthropy or love of mankind 3. The Discipline of Assent, which has to do with mindfulness of our judgements Marcus Aurelius references the disciplines a few times through *Meditations* and its clear he was influenced by Epictetus. **1. The Discipline of Desire (a.k.a. Stoic Acceptance)** The discipline of desire is the virtue of living in accordance with Nature or the Universe as a Whole. This includes having a philosophical attitude toward life and accepting our Fate as inevitable. Fate here is not some mysterious metaphysical force of predetermination. It simply means the causal network of events that bring about subsequent events (cause and effect). *Seek not for events to happen as you wish but wish events to happen as they do and your life will go smoothly and serenely.* (Enchiridion, VIII) This does not mean be a push over or live life passively (this paradox will be explained in the discipline of action). All in all, the discipline of desire is the calm acceptance of everything out of our immediate control; desiring to align that which is in our control with virtue, and not desiring that which is out of our control. **2. The Discipline of Action (Stoic Philanthropy)** According to Stoic tradition, virtue is the only good and is sufficient to live a life of fulfillment (*eudaimonia*). This discipline includes developing the four Stoic virtues and taming the four passions. The IV Virtues I. Courage - overcoming fear or aversion to what ought to be done (fortitude, bravery) II. Temperance - overcoming attracting or desire to what ought not to be done (moderation, discipline) III. Wisdom - knowing what ought to be done and ought to be avoided (discernment, right judgment) IV. Justice - thought and action resulting in the common good (morality, fairness, benevolence) The IV Passions I. Fear - irrational aversion to something falsely judged as bad (cowardice, procrastination) II. Craving - irrational attraction to something falsely judged as good (gluttony, greed, addiction) III. Pain - irrational sadness over something falsely judged as bad (moping, self-pity) IV. Elation - irrational happiness over something falsely judged as good (over-excitement, indulgence) The discipline of action is essentially undertaking all action in harmony with our fellow humans, as well as helping them flourish (i.e. live a life of *eudaimonia*), pursing actions in accordance with the virtues and avoiding the passions. Or, at least making sure our actions dont go *against* our virtues and the good of mankind. However, because the condition of others is out of our control, we should undertake these actions with a reserve clause such as Fate permitting, God-willing, etc., always remembering that our actions can be obstructed. Hence, Marcus Aurelius appears to refer to three clauses that Stoics should be continually mindful to attach to all of their actions: 1. That they are undertaken with a reserve clause (hupexairesis) 2. That they are for the common welfare of mankind (koinônikai) 3. That they accord with value (kat axian) Value is in reference to the preferred indifferents. Stoics are indifferent to what is out of their control, including life and death, health and disease, etc. However, life is preferable to death, health to disease, financial stability to poverty, etc. and thus we are allowed to pursue these things in accord with value. **3. The Discipline of Assent (Stoic Mindfulness)** The discipline of assent is the virtue of living in accordance with our nature as rational beings, which means living in accord with reason and truth in our thoughts and speech. Assent is in reference to which thoughts or impression we agree with. It consists of monitoring our inner voice and confronting our value judgements. For instance, when we hear of a death, our inner voice may say That is tragic. If we give assent to this impression, then we judge the event as tragic even though it was in accordance with nature. Instead we should catch the impression and ask Was this death truly tragic, or is it nature running its course? All things must come to an end eventually. Is that truly a tragedy? and so on. Men are not disturbed by things, but by the views which they take of things. (Enchiridion, V) (Although it can seem like doctrine, Stoicism is not a religion and shouldnt be practiced dogmatically. As always, extract what you want and apply it as you wish. This is from the original Stoic teachings and thus can be modified to fit modern practice of Stoicism. God knows I dont practice everything in this post.)

Keep in mind my mom is a single mom and has been raising me for years now , I only saw my day once and at most 5 times a year so I was not expecting him . I got to the bed , sat down and my mom gave me a very worried and concerned look but befire she could say anything my dad open his mouth ... His exact words were , "Stop being depressed, it's embarrassing me and I don't want to deal with your nonsense ." That broke my heart , I knew he didn't care but I didn't think it was that bad , I was still in my drowsy state but the moment he said that I think I might be woken up a little . The rest of the conversation with them was a blur but I just remember being so fixated on what he said to me . That was the last time we spoke , he didn't even wish me a happy birthday this year . I'm only 14 , he broke what little hope I had of us finally reuniting as daughter and dad , I didn't have alot of hope to begin with but damn. What I have come to realise [SEP] I'm going to start off by saying I am on the tail end of an existential crisis. I still have feelings of hopelessness sometimes and wonder about the point of it all. But I'll try to give a few points as I feel writing this may help someone. # Don't be so arrogant: You are one human, on one planet. Probably in a small enough community that knows a few people (or a lot depending on your viewpoint). Why are you thinking in terms of the universe? Why are you extrapolating your existence as being negligible in the "grand scheme of things"? You are human. Your grand scheme of things is the immediate area you can affect. The people around you. Oh, they'll die too? and your lives, and memories spent together will mean nothing too? Well... # You will be forgotten, but you won't: If you go out tomorrow and see someone struggling to lift luggage into their car trunk. You'll help them (hopefully). You won't think much about it afterward as you will be balls-deep in contemplating are "I and the worm is of the same importance in terms of existence". But the person you helped will think good of you, and more importantly, they will be able to achieve whatever goal it is they need to do. You being there allowed them to get their luggage in their car, therefore, they are on time at the airport, and they have not missed their flight to make their weekend away with friends. They have now arrived at their all-inclusive holiday with friends, where the person you helped has caught the eye of someone. They talk all night, they connect, and they exchange contact details. They talk more and more. They decide to give the long-distance thing a go. Hey, look at that 3 years have gone by and they have been living together for 2 of those years. They have now gotten married and have had a bunch of kids. All because the person you helped didn't miss their flight and because you decided to stop and help at that moment, at that time, because you existed. Oh yes, that couple will die, but guess what? One of those kids went on to have an illustrious career in biotech and has cured Alzheimer's. I am absolutely aware of how ludicrous this sounds. But what I am driving at is that your life is made of thousands of small encounters that have a ripple effect waaaay into the future. Beyond you. How you affect people around you, most importantly the people close to you will influence them and vice versa. Your duty is not to the universe, it is to your fellow man. You are human, your concern is not the universe, you are not a planet, you're not a solar system, you're not the fabric of the cosmos ("weeeeere all made of stardust, be quiet or I will live, laugh, love your ass"). You are human. And... # That's ok to be human: Why are we here? We're going to all fade away at some point. Aren't we? Who knows. Who knows how far we will go as a race? Who knows what we will change into? What answers we'll get? We are so fortunate to be born in a time of wonder and discovery we don't appreciate how dark the world was in terms of knowledge. We have the arrogance to us to assume we don't have the answers now when things are so good that we will never have the answers. There's a prevailing attitude of we will never get "it". But you are in service of our species. Imagine a world working in harmony in a few hundred years even. We are in the 21st century and have hangovers from the 20th century and preceding centuries. Can we work it out? Can we find the common ground to combine together to work in true harmony? Yes of course we can. Late 19th century Europe was divided into colonial powers by the end of the 20th century Western Europe as a united entity was a realised dream. And most likely, will stay like that. In an age of ever-increasing travel and communication, we are understanding each other more or with other places hashing out differences. Your duty is to be a good person, to act morally, ethically and with conviction. Because the people before you did. To give you this. Yes it is still all a bit messy and worrisome at the moment but we are so far removed from where we were 200 years ago it is amazing. All because our ancestors said "you know what? we can do better" We certainly have a way to go, but do not think of yourself as a spec of a spec in the universe. You are a drop in the ocean of the human race. We all are. We are all together the wave of change we want to be. I don't know about you but I am proud of that. It is enough to know you did good in your time as a person, to know you made a difference to people. I hark back to my previous point of helping even just one person. If we all adopt this attitude if we all continue to persist this is the way to exist and progress where do you think we will be in a few hundred years? # Oh but come on it is still pointless: Aw sorry, you have to die and everything is indeed going to end. But there is a surreal quality to it isn't there? To exist here, in these conditions, with life happening. I mean evolution explains a lot right? But why does evolution work like some algorithm continuously learning, changing over millions of years? That's a bit odd and specific isn't it, that it would work like that. That billions of life forms would somehow work in harmony eventually. That there is a perfect balance of matter, time, gravity and events making this whole reality just work. Then it all ends, but how did it start? I am not going to melt your head into a 404 error but I will say this. There is no one thing that can explain it all. So for me. At least. There is some point to it. There is some reason the universe is here. That in itself gives me comfort. I can't make heads nor tails of it and neither will you or anyone who tells you otherwise. Genius or not. We are not there yet. You can only get so much perspective on what a place is like when you see it from your own Tv (Earth). Without leaving to see what it's like yourself. So what does this mean? Your existence is not in the perspective of those things, so think smaller. And when you start thinking of the scary scale of things and existence. Well. Think of why existence put us here. I am not going to say some entity or whatever put us here. But you can more than rationally tie the point of the universe did put us here, in a very specific way, but why. And more importantly why are we able to appreciate it? # You want to go on but you don't: I believe. If you live a good rich life, helping others and in your last days have people who are living better lives because of you. You have completed life. Yes, potential oblivion awaits, or maybe not. Don't let anyone say what is and isn't after, consciousness is a whole other discussion and this is a subjective thing for each person (sorry I can't plug that hole). But it is one of our main what the hell is that doing there subjects we deal with today. But discussions around continuation or part of a larger reality abound. So I'm just highlighting. Food for thought, skepticism for both points of view. But one hand in each pot is my advice. But I'll tell you how I got over this wall (of China). I have contemplated and lived in each eventuality. I have played in my mind what it would be like to go into nothingness (I hate the term oblivion, relax, it's death, you will not be there Shakespeare). You have probably heard oh it'll be just like before you were born. Yeah, except I didn't have a concept of self and living then did I? I have learned to treat death as this irritating thing I just have to do. Like a house chore, I have diminished it, because if there is nothing else after it is simply a non-event. Just a case of ok let's just get it done. I have put it on my list of the least important things to do. I won't be able to even think oh this is pretty awful. Then...I have thought about what it would be like to go on. I looked at NDEs, I looked at the reality of consciousness, and I pondered questions on why the heck are we just even here. Is there a plane of reality where we exist elsewhere? Another universe we go into after all this? Is there a higher purpose? So where did this leave me? Agnostic. Hopeful that there might be something after, fine (sometimes comforted?) that there's nothing after. And you know what this done. It brought me right back to here and now. It made me want to live life, to do good, to be an optimistic person, and to believe that we will find our grand purpose and conquer ourselves and our reality. # So to conclude: It's irrational, but I do think we are going to discover mind-bending, space-farting things as a species. I don't see why not. We had 50-60 years from the first airplane to landing on the moon as just a small example. I see that as our ultimate point in living. To be kind to one another, to bring understanding to each other, and to progress this thing we call humanity. I feel good when I help someone, don't you? My life is a process of driving out my ego and replacing it with satisfaction I got good utility value out of my life. I think it's easy to get in our heads it's all pointless, but ground yourself. Give your life perspective to here and now, how it does serve to affect things in multiple inexplicable ways. And understand the mystery of the universe/reality. How anything is possible, how nothing is a given, not even death. Life is not one big distraction before the inevitable. It is a gift that you get to use to help others and of course, have loads of fun on the way. Write, create, live, laugh, love (I told you I would live, laugh, love your ass). We and all of this has to go. But how it goes. Well, I believe that is up to us. You, me and no one knows how far we can go. On a more practical note. Sleep, eat well, and always be near people when you're feeling like this. We are so buried in our screens and not ever here in the present. This is probably the most common advice but so, so, so essential. Look after your body and you look after your mind. This is literally the reason I can write more than what I think is an optimistic outlook on existence. Having basically sat around the last few months getting fat. It changed my mindset. You won't always feel like this. I am a living example of this.

While it's already quite fascinating there's so few organic matter in such a big universe of dead matter, dark matter or no matter, even more fascinating it is why we rare humans have a much wider set of abilities than we would need for surviving and reproduction. Let's assume this is an overage and let's not just raise the arguments that evolution brought reproduction benefits through cleverness and cultural behavior. This overage... It's the root cause of our spiritual search, our demand for philosophy, our ability to ask and also guilty for our regret to lack of an answer. It's comfortable and satisfying to expect that this ability overage is our unique selling point, raising ourselves to something bigger, to something important - if not THE important key of everything. People are waiting for the future, hoping to reach the next level, transcendence, hope that we don't extinct before. What about the idea that we're here to fulfill a truthful function, a deeper meaning for our existence. However - not that romantic and not with us as the pride of creation. What if we are some kind of supercluster. Synapses of a greater good. Pieces of a machine, or more likely an organism. Nothing that we could name, such as a bacteria that can't imagine the body that contains the guts it's living in. That would somehow explain why we have this extra capacity. That we have free resources to calculate maths and think over and over about physics, about philosophy, about that imaginary theory of everything. What if exactly this is our function, our task. We are probably in an intermediate state of a program - an AI that is designed to solve a problem - or to evolve. Let's not get into the matrix and simulation discussions that lead to infinite regress and are not providing a satisfying answer. I try to find an explanation for our ability to think. That ability that separates us from anything else we know. Our fantasy. That extra resources we seem to have for a reason we don't see. How could we use this more productive? How could we find our function? How could we serve the reason for our existence? And would we even be able to break our limits and find the greater reason? Could we as an AI evolve into something better? Is that maybe our purpose? Could a bacteria evolve to a level clever enough to understand its position in our body? And what would that lead to? Life is a TV show [SEP] Life is like a tv show. It starts, it gets good. It has downs... but you fall in love with it. Some go on for a long time and some end quickly. But it ends. It has to. If it didn't end then it would get boring. You'd look at the tv show and think "this is just the same stuff but re-written". And that's the thing with life. It's people looking into life and finding a reason to be there. To find excitement and find enjoyment. After a time they accomplish this and can live until they die. And the cycle repeats. Another person watching a new tv show finding a reason to finish it. The meaning of life is nothing but a basic, natural instinct to reproduce. To keep the Species going to "watch more TV shows". So if it's just going to end and the only reason to be here is to keep the Species going then what's the point? There is none. However you can read this is two lights. The side, such as myself, who sees it as a free opportunity to go out and enjoy what you do and to find new and wondrous things to explore. Take every day as if it's the final episode... or... You can look at it as there's no reason to be in this loop, only certain that death is how it ends. That's how I used to be. Thinking that life wasn't anything more than being around and dying. But if you remember the TV shows, they have exciting parts and sad parts throughout them. Your favourite characters die. Some get together with who you "shipped" and some leave and never come back. You get to experience all this and find more and more reasons to stick about. Currently I'm at an impasse with emotion. Confident that I know that life is amazing and terrible because you know that the show has to end, but know that if it didn't you'd get bored. You'd run out of stuff to watch and get excited about. You also know that everyone you love with eventually end too. But remember what I said before? They were practically the same but there was stuff in the middle of the loop and dying. That stuff in the middle is the reason to carry on with the loop. To find enjoyment and to watch people grow. Death is scary and it's horrifying. But at the same time. It's beautiful. That person's show has gotten to its final episode and the story can't go on any longer. I experience a feeling of no other. I couldn't explain how I felt. There is no word for the feeling to my knowledge but this is what came of it. It may have been an epiphany but I feel like it was much deeper than that. It was a strong wave of emotion. The feeling at this point has come and gone but I've gotten this from watching the good place. I watched the final chapter and realised that there's so much to life. But yet so little. You can experience as much as you want but every experience is the same. You stand up in a crowd and do the thing you've always wanted to do. The feelings rush and wash over you. And then it fades. And you look for the next thing to do. If I get the feeling again I'll update. That is if people want to hear more. Sorry for the long post

The semantics of the term "free will" are NOT up for debate when discussed in the context of metaphysics and philosophy [SEP] It interests me really, why would we be so split on which definition is best for free will? I'm not saying you're wrong but the way I understand it is that free will should be separated from "will." We all possess a will. Will: We have desires, wants, beliefs, motivations, intuitions, and reasons to do what we do. We possess the ability to choose what we want and act the way we want. It's our volition, it's our will, and the choice is ours as well. The word free is always used to denote the negation or absence of the influence of something. Say, for example, that I buy a book and the shop gives me one more for free. Free of charge, that's what free means in this context. Being released from prison would, for example, mean free of typical prison duties, prison guards, and prison restrictions that can impede a person's actions. Your locus of personal freedom (acting as per your volition) shrinks when your surroundings contain agents who posses "well-being threatening" amounts power of action **and**, more importantly, desires, motivations, and beliefs that conflict with your own. Environments that threaten well-being (like living in a desert or in a low-income household with abusive parents) also produce a similar effect. Free will does not refer to a sort of magical ability that we possess, it merely states that our wills are free off something, and *that* something seems to be the root cause of this whole confusion over the semantics of free will. Now, we can be free of being enslaved by other human beings, free from being threatened by a criminal, free from being forced by a person or something in our environment or an illness inside our bodies to do whatever we want. That's personal liberty and basic/optimum humans rights/living conditions. But when you're talking heavy duty metaphysics, you're talking about the philosophical notion of free will in the context of determinism being the opposing view. Are human thoughts, choices, and actions free of causes that are not initiated or caused by the agent themselves? And the answer is very clear. Either they are not, in which case it would mean that our wills are not free of said causes, or the alternative scenario where we do author the thoughts, desires, and reasons that directly lead to our decisions and actions, but that will make you fall into an infinite regress since at some point across the chain of thoughts and wills, they'd have either spawned randomly out of thin air (or hopefully neurobiology can figure it out) or you must provide newer links to the chain of reason and thoughtÓ_x000F_ which results in an infinite regress. We possess wills but our wills aren't the product of causes initiated/caused by us, the agent. Our wills aren't free of being caused by prior causes that we aren't responsible for. Either that or our wills possess some quasi quantum-mechanical properties and pop up from thin air until they become apparent and intelligible to us.

A second or a lifetime? Does it matter? Does it all matter? [SEP] When you're younger the world is so simple. You view life upwards as so far away. You're immortal. But when I hit 30 (currently 36 at the time of writing this) I had a brutal existential crisis, which still effects me most days. For context, I'm an atheist. I have no problem with people following a religion, but looking at the world, I just can't believe there is a magic afterlife. I'm jealous of people with that comfort. Side note, I used to work in a Cathedral and would often walk through the Nave thinking "God, if you're there, in a super holy place, give me a sign" but I never felt anything. However our Dean was once a sound engineer and heard God tell her to become a priest... One day, I was laying in bed at night in the dark and thinking about death, which I guess was triggered by the shock of turning 30. For one split second I imagined what it would be like not to exist after death. It scared the shit out of me and for the next year or two I had a super bad existential crisis. --------------------------- It made me seriously ponder a question: "is there a difference between living one second or 100 years?" --------------------------- This feeling, still hits me often, usually at night and it is like having my guts sucked out of me with a cold wave. I guess I'm describing that cold wave you get when you remember something terrible. I thought I had turned a corner from it but it's always in the back of my mind when I see someone die on a film or a series on TV. I feel sad for the passing of life. Its actually been one of the driving forces behind going vegan (I was already veggie), as I can't stand living creatures losing their right to exist for me to eat. I've got a good life, love my work, got great friends, travel the world and importantly I have a loving partner and a wonderful relationship. I guess this is something I'll never get over.
